claims.text: Sliding friction can dynamically produce an ultra-nanocrystalline or nano-amorphous near-surface layer in high-entropy alloys.
Formation of the dynamically reorganized near-surface layer increases local hardness.
Formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer is associated with reduced friction.
Formation of the reorganized near-surface layer lowers wear rate.
High-entropy-alloy protective coatings can be deposited by atmospheric plasma spraying.
The relevant as-deposited high-entropy-alloy coating has a relatively coarse-grained microstructure.
Annealing or surface hardening can stabilize the initial coarse-grained structure and suppress or delay friction-induced grain refinement.
Using an inert or low-oxidation environment can reduce oxide-film contributions and help isolate mechanically driven wear behavior.
Reduced near-surface grain size or amorphous features can be used as evidence of dynamic surface reorganization.
Sliding-induced shear drives the surface transformation from a coarse-grained state to an ultra-nanocrystalline or partially amorphous state.
The transformed surface accommodates plastic deformation through grain-boundary-mediated mechanisms.
The transformed surface suppresses material removal.
Coatings pretreated to inhibit dynamic surface nanostructuring will have higher friction coefficients than untreated coatings.
Coatings pretreated to inhibit dynamic surface nanostructuring will have higher wear rates than untreated coatings.
Untreated material should develop a nanoscale near-surface layer correlated with superior wear resistance.
The proposed mechanism should govern wear under moderate sliding loads and speeds when oxidation is minimized or secondary.
High temperature or strongly oxidizing conditions can introduce oxidation, phase transformation, or oxide-nanocomposite wear mechanisms.
In reactive environments, oxide-nanocomposite formation may contribute independently to wear resistance.
